Nice, that puts you at an interesting point academically.
If you're entering 3rd year of the BITS–RMIT program, you've already completed:
2 years at BITS
Core first- and second-year engineering/math/CS foundations
You're about to transition into the more specialized phase of the degree
Based on what you've told me before, your situation roughly looks like:
What you already have
Strong English (IELTS 8, TOEFL 104)
CS background from BITS
Upcoming courses like OOP, PLCC, Discrete Structures, Logic, Digital Design
Interest in:
Machine Learning
DSA
Potentially quant/HFT preparation
Making money online through a laptop
What becomes important now
Companies don't care that much about first-year CG anymore. By the end of 3rd year they mainly look at:
Projects
Internships
DSA skills
CGPA
Specialized skills (ML, systems, web, etc.)
If I were planning the next 2 years
Tier 1: Maintain CG
Try to keep your CG healthy. Don't sacrifice academics completely for side hustles.
Tier 2: DSA
By the end of 3rd year:
Arrays
Strings
Linked Lists
Trees
Graphs
DP
Greedy
Heaps
Aim for ~200–300 quality problems rather than chasing huge numbers.
Tier 3: One specialization
Pick one primary track:
Option A: Software Engineering
OOP
DBMS
OS
Networks
Full-stack projects
Option B: ML/AI
Python
NumPy
Pandas
ML fundamentals
Deep Learning
Projects
Option C: Quant
Probability
Statistics
Mental math
DSA
Competitive programming
Trying to do all three seriously at once usually leads to mediocre progress.
Biggest mistake I see BITS students make
They spend:
100 hours watching career videos
50 hours making roadmaps
10 hours actually coding
The students who get good internships usually just build stuff consistently for a year.
Since you're entering Year 3, I'd start thinking in terms of:
"What do I want recruiters to see on my resume 12 months from now?"
That answer should guide what you spend your free time on this semester.
Out of software engineering, ML, and quant, which one attracts you the most right now? That changes the optimal plan quite a bit.
i'll be in rmit, how are the courses over there?
Bro, as someone coming from BITS, I think you'll notice a pretty big difference in teaching style at RMIT University.
The good stuff
1. Much more project-oriented
RMIT heavily pushes project-based learning through its Bootcamp2Studio model. Instead of endless lectures and theory-heavy exams, you'll often learn a concept and immediately build something with it. They emphasize team projects, hackathons, industry-style workflows, and capstone projects.
RMIT University
+1
For a BITS student, it can feel like:
Less "prove this theorem"
More "build this system"
2. Industry focus is strong
RMIT's computing programs are designed with industry input and cover areas like:
Cloud computing
Security
Web systems
Mobile computing
Big data
Application development
Industry projects and work-integrated learning are a major theme.
RMIT University
+1
3. Internships matter
One thing RMIT is known for is the Professional degrees that include substantial industry placement/internship opportunities. Their software engineering and professional computer science pathways emphasize a long internship component and industry networking.
RMIT University
+2
RMIT University
+2
The not-so-good stuff
1. Less theoretical depth than BITS
If you're used to:
MATH F111/F112
Discrete Mathematics
Formal proofs
Heavy derivations
then some RMIT courses may feel less rigorous mathematically and more applied.
A common student sentiment is that you often need to self-learn deeper theory if you're interested in it.
Reddit
+1
2. Self-learning is expected
Several students mention that the university gives the framework, but a lot of growth comes from independent study. Good students thrive; passive students can coast and learn relatively little.
Reddit
+1
For YOU specifically
Based on what I know:
You're a BITS CS student.
You're interested in ML.
You want DSA.
You've thought about quant/HFT.
You're already stronger in math than the average CS student.
Your biggest challenge at RMIT probably won't be academics.
It'll be using the extra freedom wisely.
Many exchange/transfer students arrive thinking:
"Courses are easier than BITS, life is chill."
Then they waste a year.
The smarter move is:
Keep CGPA healthy.
Grind DSA seriously.
Build 2–3 strong projects.
Get internship experience in Australia.
Network aggressively.
If you do that, the RMIT years can actually be more valuable for employability than another two years of pure theory.
One thing I'm curious about: in the BITS–RMIT pathway, are you going into Computer Science, Software Engineering, or another specialization at RMIT? That determines what your exact course list will look like.
these are my upcoming 2 years
Bro, looking at this curriculum, I'd say it's actually a pretty solid Software Engineering degree, but it's very different from the traditional CS route.
Year 3
Computer Architecture and Organization
This is your low-level systems course.
You'll likely cover:
CPU architecture
Instruction sets
Memory hierarchy
Cache
Pipelines
Assembly basics
This is one of the most valuable courses if you ever want:
Systems programming
OS
Embedded
Performance engineering
System Architecture and Design
This is basically:
"How do you design large software systems?"
Topics typically include:
Requirements analysis
UML
Design patterns
Software architecture
Client-server systems
Scalability concepts
Useful for actual industry work.
Algorithm and Analysis
This is the course I would pay the most attention to.
Expect:
Time complexity
Recurrence relations
Sorting
Graphs
Dynamic Programming
Greedy algorithms
This is probably the closest thing you'll have to interview-prep material.
If you master this course and continue LeetCode alongside it, you'll be in a good position for internships.
Embedded System Design and Implementation
You'll likely work with:
Microcontrollers
Sensors
Real hardware
Can be fun but can also be annoying when hardware refuses to cooperate.
Full Stack Development
Very employable.
Expect:
Frontend
Backend
APIs
Databases
Deployment
This course alone can lead to portfolio projects.
Network Fundamentals and Applications
Important.
Topics usually:
TCP/IP
Routing
Switching
DNS
HTTP
Network security basics
Useful for interviews and system design.
Software Engineering Design
A continuation of software architecture concepts.
Think:
Team projects
Documentation
Design methodologies
Agile development
Year 4
Computing Theory
This is your theoretical CS course.
Expect:
Automata
DFA/NFA
Regular languages
Context-free grammars
Turing machines
Computability
Since you're taking Logic in CS at BITS before going, this should feel familiar.
Operating Systems Principles
One of the best courses in the whole degree.
You'll likely study:
Processes
Threads
Scheduling
Synchronization
Deadlocks
Memory management
Virtual memory
Extremely useful for:
Interviews
Systems engineering
Backend roles
Software Testing
Industry-focused course.
Topics:
Unit testing
Integration testing
Test automation
QA methodologies
Very practical.
Engineering Capstone Project A & B
Probably the most important part of the degree.
Recruiters often care more about this than 5 random courses.
Choose the project carefully.
Good examples:
ML application
Distributed system
Full-stack SaaS
Computer vision project
Embedded + AI project
Embedded Systems: OS and Interfacing
Continuation of embedded work.
Useful if you like hardware.
Software Engineering: Process and Tools
Think:
Git
CI/CD
DevOps
Agile
Project management
Stuff you'll actually use in industry.
What I think is missing
Compared to a strong CS curriculum, I don't see dedicated courses for:
❌ Databases
❌ Machine Learning
❌ Artificial Intelligence
❌ Advanced Mathematics
❌ Computer Graphics
❌ Compilers
❌ Distributed Systems
❌ Advanced Networking
❌ Cybersecurity
So if you want ML or top software roles, you'll need some self-study.
For your goals specifically
From what you've told me over the last year:
Interested in ML
Interested in DSA
Potentially interested in quant/HFT
Strong English
Coming from BITS
I'd use RMIT like this:
Priority 1
Get strong at:
Algorithms
OS
Networks
Computer Architecture
These four are gold for interviews.
Priority 2
Use Full Stack Development to build real projects.
Priority 3
Self-study ML because the curriculum doesn't seem to provide much of it.
Priority 4
Use Capstone to create something impressive enough to sit at the top of your resume.
Overall, I'd give this curriculum:
Industry preparedness: 8.5/10
Theoretical CS depth: 6.5/10
Employability: 8.5/10
Preparation for ML research: 5/10
Preparation for software engineering roles: 9/10
The biggest opportunity for you is that these courses are generally less mathematically brutal than many BITS courses, so you can use the extra bandwidth to seriously build up DSA, ML, and internships while you're in Australia.
